question: What has nobody measured yet for recycled-paper reject fibre as a PHA feedstock?

claims.text: No measurement of PHA production on recycled-paper reject fibre is in the corpus: no titre, content, or productivity was found for that feedstock in any strain or process.
Glucose-rich hydrolyzate from pulp and paper mill sludge, not reject fibre, was used as the sole carbon source for PHA production by Bacillus thuringiensis in cyclic fed-batch cultivation.

passages.quote: This study reports the practicality of employing Bacillus thuringiensis in a CFBF cultivation using glucose-rich hydrolyzate derived from enzymatic saccharification of pulp and paper mill sludge as the sole carbon source.

gaps: PHA titre, PHA content and productivity measured on recycled-paper reject fibre, either as raw material or after hydrolysis, in any production host.
Composition of reject fibre (cellulose, hemicellulose, ash, plastic and coating contaminants) and how it varies between mills; the corpus has no characterisation of this stream.
Enzymatic or acid saccharification yield of reject fibre and any inhibitor profile, measured against the PHA-producing strain.
Strain-level tests of whether a PHA producer grows on reject-fibre hydrolysate, including any sugar-utilisation or toxicity data.
Mixed-culture PHA results on reject fibre; the corpus has paper mill sludge and wastewater work but none on reject fibre.
A minimum selling price or techno-economic run for a reject-fibre PHA process; none exists in the corpus.
A yield ceiling for PHA from reject-fibre sugars: the yield-ceiling tool covers only glucose, fructose and xylose and I did not run it.

passages.heading: Introduction
passages.text: The CFBF process entails the partial withdrawal of fermentation medium and subsequent re-filling with an equal volume of fresh fermentation medium. The chemical composition of the fermentation medium must be consistent throughout the "empty-and-fill" process. The CFBF strategy prevents increases in concentrations of toxic by-products and enhances cell growth to achieve high concentrations of final biomass and increased PHA yields (Ibrahim and Steinbüchel 2010; Gahlawat and Srivastava 2018). This study reports the practicality of employing Bacillus thuringiensis in a CFBF cultivation using glucose-rich hydrolyzate derived from enzymatic saccharification of pulp and paper mill sludge as the sole carbon source. Firstly, a statistical optimization study was conducted to elucidate the optimal fermentation medium to produce high cell density biomass.
